observation.transcript:
A Contributor License Agreement (CLA) grants a project the legal right to use and distribute your code. To derive or build your own from an existing protocol like the Hexagonal Contributor License (HCL), you must take the core clauses—such as intellectual property retention, no-consequence exit rights, and patent grants—and adapt them to fit your project's specific needs. [[1](https://opensource.stackexchange.com/questions/15766/licensing-rights-of-an-only-contributor-into-a-no-license-github-repository-cre), [2](https://livingarchitecturelab.org/about/contributor-license/), [3](https://hexdocs.pm/ream/license.html), [4](https://neo4j.com/developer/cla/)]
4 Steps to Derive Your Own Contributor License

1. Review Existing Baselines: Read the [Living Architecture Lab HCL v3.0](https://livingarchitecturelab.org/about/contributor-license/) or examine the [Zenodo Hexagonal Contributor License v1.0](https://zenodo.org/records/19656151) for reference. [1](https://zenodo.org/records/19656151)
2. Define IP Ownership: State clearly that contributors retain their intellectual property while only granting the project the right to distribute it. [1](https://livingarchitecturelab.org/about/contributor-license/)
3. Include Patent Grants: Add standard language so contributors promise not to sue the project or its users for patent infringement. [[1](https://cyberpanel.net/blog/gpl-license-open-source-freedom), [2](https://hexdocs.pm/ream/license.html)]
4. Establish Exit Rights: Define the conditions under which a contributor can revoke their license or leave the project without negative consequences. [1](https://livingarchitecturelab.org/about/contributor-license/)
How clis/protocols handle these licenses
If you are automating license tracking and tracking what dependencies your project is using, you can use compatibility-checking tools like [GitHub Licenseal](https://github.com/shcherbak-ai/licenseal) to check the compliance of packages. [1](https://github.com/shcherbak-ai/licenseal)
Could you tell me:

* What kind of project are you writing this for (open-source software, creative writing, or engineering)?
* Do you want contributors to have commercial or non-commercial rights?
I can help you fill in the specific legal clauses you need.
